questions.question: Translate: 'All birds can fly except penguins.'
questions.solutionApproach: Let Bird(x), Fly(x), Penguin(x). 'All birds that are not penguins can fly': ∀x((Bird(x)∧¬Penguin(x))→Fly(x)).

questions.question: Translate: 'Every student has taken at least one course taught by every professor in the CS department.' (this is intentionally ambiguous — give the reading where a single course works for ALL professors)
questions.solutionApproach: Let S(x)=student, P(y)=professor, C(z)=course, Taught(y,z), Taken(x,z). Strong reading (same course for all professors): ∀x(S(x)→∃z(C(z)∧∀y(P(y)→Taught(y,z))∧Taken(x,z))).
questions.answer: ∀x(S(x)→∃z(C(z)∧∀y(P(y)→Taught(y,z))∧Taken(x,z))) — note ∃z is OUTSIDE ∀y here, meaning one course taught by every professor.

questions.question: Is ∀x∃y P(x,y) equivalent to ∃y∀x P(x,y)? Justify with a concrete example over the domain of integers, P(x,y) = 'y is greater than x'.
questions.solutionApproach: ∀x∃y P(x,y): for every integer x, there's SOME bigger y — TRUE (always find x+1). ∃y∀x P(x,y): there's ONE y bigger than EVERY integer x — FALSE (no largest bound). So NOT equivalent; ∃y∀x is strictly stronger and false here while ∀x∃y is true.
questions.answer: Not equivalent. ∀x∃y P(x,y) is TRUE but ∃y∀x P(x,y) is FALSE for this example — proves ∃∀ ⟹ ∀∃ but not conversely.

questions.question: Is the formula ∃x∀y (R(x,y)↔¬R(y,y)) satisfiable over some domain? (This is Russell's-paradox-flavored.)
questions.solutionApproach: Set y=x: R(x,x)↔¬R(x,x) — this is a direct contradiction (a statement equivalent to its own negation), forced by the universal quantifier over y including y=x. So the formula is UNSATISFIABLE in any domain.
questions.answer: No — unsatisfiable in any domain (the y=x instantiation forces a direct contradiction, same structure as Russell's Paradox).
